title: Decisive battles of the 20th century
note: Five battles show recurring strategic patterns: the Marne (1914) wrecked a plan built on speed and timetables; Stalingrad (1942 to 1943) turned an overextended offensive into an encirclement; Midway (1942) turned on intelligence and minutes; Normandy (1944) combined deception, logistics and mass; Inchon (1950) struck far behind an enemy's front.

read.title: Five turning points
text: In 1914 Germany's Schlieffen Plan bet everything on speed: swing through Belgium, take Paris, then turn east. Friction and fatigue wore down the marching armies, a gap opened between two of them, and at the Marne the French and British counterattacked. The plan failed, and the war settled into trenches.

At Stalingrad in 1942, a German offensive aimed at Caucasus oil became bogged down in street fighting. The Soviets massed reserves and in November struck the weakly held flanks, trapping the Sixth Army, which surrendered early in 1943 when supply by air proved hopeless.

At Midway in June 1942, American codebreakers learned Japan's plan, and US carrier aircraft sank four Japanese carriers, ending Japan's offensive momentum in the Pacific. Two years later, the Normandy landings of June 6, 1944 combined deception that fixed German attention on Calais, artificial harbors, and overwhelming air and naval power.

In September 1950, with UN forces penned in around Pusan, Douglas MacArthur landed at Inchon, deep behind North Korean lines, despite dangerous tides. Seoul fell quickly. But the advance north that followed provoked Chinese intervention, a reminder that a brilliant operation can lead into a strategic trap.
